chapter.title: TypeScript
chapter.summary: Using the type system to prevent bugs: structural typing, narrowing, generics, utility and mapped types, and practical configuration.

lessons.title: The TypeScript type system: structural typing, unions and narrowing
lessons.summary: How TypeScript checks types structurally, the difference between any, unknown and never, union and intersection types, narrowing, discriminated unions and exhaustive checks.

parts.label: Types and structure
parts.body:
## What TypeScript is (and isn't)

TypeScript is JavaScript plus a **static type checker**. The compiler analyses your code, reports mismatches before it runs, then **erases** all types, producing plain JavaScript. Consequences you must remember:

- Types **do not exist at runtime**. You can't `typeof x === "MyInterface"`. Validate untrusted data at runtime (zod, valibot) and let types describe the result.
- TypeScript can be **unsound** on purpose (casts, `any`, array index access without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`). Types describe what you *believe*; the compiler checks consistency, not truth.
- Compile-time errors don't stop JavaScript from running; your build decides whether they block deployment (they should).

## Structural typing

TypeScript compares types by **shape**, not by name ("duck typing, checked at compile time"). If an object has the required properties with compatible types, it is assignable, no `implements` required.

```ts
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
function norm(p: Point) { return Math.hypot(p.x, p.y); }
const v = { x: 3, y: 4, label: "v" };
norm(v);                  // OK: extra property is fine for a variable (not a fresh literal)
norm({ x: 3, y: 4, label: "v" });   // error: excess property check applies to fresh object literals
```

Two differently named types with the same shape are interchangeable. If you need nominal-style safety (UserId vs OrderId, both strings) use **branded types**:

```ts
type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" };
const asUserId = (s: string) => s as UserId;
```

## Core types

- Primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint`, `symbol`, `null`, `undefined`.
- Arrays `number[]` / `Array<number>`; tuples `[string, number]` (fixed length and positions; labelled `[name: string, age: number]`).
- Object types and `interface`s; function types `(a: number) => string`.
- **Literal types**: `"GET"`, `42`, `true`. With `as const` an object/array becomes readonly with literal types.
- **`enum`** exists but a union of string literals is usually lighter and erases cleanly: `type Role = "admin" | "user"`.
- **`type` vs `interface`**: both describe objects. Interfaces can be extended and **merged** (declaration merging) and produce better error messages for objects; `type` aliases can name unions, tuples, mapped and conditional types. Pick one convention (interface for public object shapes, type for everything else is common).

## any, unknown, never, void

| type | meaning | use |
|---|---|---|
| `any` | opt out of checking entirely | avoid; it spreads silently |
| `unknown` | a value of **unknown type**; you must narrow before use | the safe `any`: use for parsed JSON, `catch (e)`, external input |
| `never` | no value can occur | functions that always throw; impossible branches (exhaustiveness) |
| `void` | function returns nothing useful | return type of callbacks that ignore results |

Turn on `"strict": true`. It enables `strictNullChecks` (so `null`/`undefined` aren't silently assignable to everything, the largest source of runtime errors prevented), `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes`, and others. Also consider `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (indexing returns `T | undefined`), `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` and `noImplicitOverride`.

parts.label: Unions and narrowing
Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

TypeScript questions probe whether you use types to **model the domain** and prevent bugs, versus sprinkling `any` and `as`.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. `any` vs `unknown`?

**Model answer.** `any` turns off type checking for a value and for everything derived from it. `unknown` is the type-safe counterpart: anything can be assigned to it, but you must narrow it (typeof, instanceof, a type guard or schema validation) before using it. I use `unknown` for parsed JSON, caught errors and external input, and keep `any` out of the codebase with lint rules.

### 2. `interface` vs `type`?

**Model answer.** Both describe object shapes and are often interchangeable. Interfaces support declaration merging and `extends`, and give clearer errors for object types; type aliases can also express unions, intersections, tuples, mapped and conditional types. I follow the team convention, typically interface for object contracts and type for unions and computed types.

### 3. What is structural typing?

**Model answer.** Compatibility is determined by the shape of a type, not its declared name: an object is assignable if it has the required members with compatible types. It makes TypeScript flexible with JavaScript's patterns, but means two unrelated types of the same shape are interchangeable, so I use branded types when I need to distinguish IDs or units.

### 4. What is a discriminated union and why is it useful?

**Model answer.** A union of object types that share a literal-typed tag property. Checking the tag narrows the type in each branch, so only valid properties are accessible, and a `never` check in the default branch makes the compiler flag unhandled variants. It models state machines and API results so illegal states are unrepresentable.

### 5. What does `strict` enable and why does `strictNullChecks` matter?

**Model answer.** A bundle of checks including `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply` and more. `strictNullChecks` stops `null` and `undefined` from being assignable to every type, forcing explicit handling of missing values, which removes the most common runtime error (cannot read property of undefined).

### 6. How do you handle data from an API in a typed way?

**Model answer.** Types vanish at runtime, so I validate the response with a runtime schema (zod, valibot) and derive the static type from it (`z.infer`). Casting the result of `res.json()` to a type is wishful thinking; if the server changes, the type lies and bugs surface later and elsewhere.

### 7. What does `satisfies` do?

**Model answer.** It checks that an expression conforms to a type without changing the expression's inferred type. That keeps literal keys and values (for example, the exact route names) while still catching mistakes, unlike a type annotation, which widens to the annotated type.

## Rapid-fire

- **Are types available at runtime?** No, they're erased.
- **Safest type for a caught error?** `unknown`.
- **How to enforce handling every union case?** Assign to `never` in the default branch.
- **`as const` does what?** Readonly with literal types.
- **Tuple vs array?** Fixed length and per-position types vs variable length.

keyPoints: TypeScript is a compile-time checker whose types are erased; validate untrusted data at runtime and derive types from the schema.
Typing is structural: compatible shape means assignable; use branded types where identity matters.
Prefer unknown over any, enable strict, and narrow with typeof, instanceof, in, equality and user-defined guards.
Discriminated unions with a literal tag plus a never exhaustiveness check make illegal states unrepresentable.
Use as const and satisfies for config objects instead of widening annotations or unchecked casts.

options: You must narrow an unknown value before using it, while any skips all checks
check.q: Why is unknown safer than any?
check.why: unknown forces a type check or validation before use; any allows arbitrary operations and spreads silently.

options: The compiler errors if a union variant is not handled
check.q: What does a never assignment in a switch default achieve?
check.why: If a new variant is added and not handled, the remaining type is not never, so assigning it to a never variable fails to compile.

options: No, extra properties are always errors
Yes, because TypeScript is structurally typed (excess property checks apply only to fresh literals)
check.q: An object { a: 1, b: 2 } is passed where { a: number } is expected from a variable. Does it compile?
check.why: Assignability depends on required members; extra properties are allowed for non-literal values.

lessons.title: Generics, utility types, mapped and conditional types
lessons.summary: Writing reusable typed code with generics and constraints, the built-in utility types, keyof and mapped types, conditional types with infer, and template literal types.

parts.label: Generics
Utility and mapped types
parts.body:
## Built-in utility types

| utility | result | example use |
|---|---|---|
| `Partial<T>` | all properties optional | PATCH bodies |
| `Required<T>` | all required | after applying defaults |
| `Readonly<T>` | all readonly | immutable state |
| `Pick<T, K>` | only keys K | public subset of a model |
| `Omit<T, K>` | everything except K | drop `password` |
| `Record<K, V>` | object with keys K and values V | lookup tables |
| `Exclude<U, X>` / `Extract<U, X>` | remove / keep union members | filter a union |
| `NonNullable<T>` | remove `null` and `undefined` | after a check |
| `ReturnType<F>` / `Parameters<F>` | a function's return / parameter types | derive types from code |
| `Awaited<T>` | unwrap a Promise | async return types |

```ts
interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; password: string }
type PublicUser = Omit<User, "password">;
type UserPatch = Partial<Pick<User, "name" | "email">>;
type CreateUser = Omit<User, "id">;
```

Deriving types from a single source of truth (a schema, a function, a const object) keeps them from drifting: `type Config = typeof defaultConfig`, `type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number]` with `const ROLES = ["admin", "user"] as const`.

## Mapped types

Transform every property of a type with `[K in keyof T]`:

```ts
type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };   // key remapping
type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };    // -readonly / -? remove modifiers
```

`Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick` and `Record` are all mapped types.

## Conditional types and infer

`T extends U ? X : Y` chooses a type based on a relationship; `infer` captures a part of a type during matching.

```ts
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type A = ElementOf<string[]>;                    // string
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T;
type Fn = (a: number, b: string) => boolean;
type Ret = Fn extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;   // boolean (this is ReturnType)
```

Conditional types **distribute** over unions: `ToArray<string | number>` becomes `string[] | number[]`; wrap in `[T]` to prevent it.

## Template literal types

```ts
type Method = "GET" | "POST";
type Path = "/users" | "/orders";
type Endpoint = `${Method} ${Path}`;     // "GET /users" | "GET /orders" | "POST /users" | "POST /orders"
type EventName<T extends string> = `on${Capitalize<T>}`;
```

Powerful for typed event names, route params and CSS-in-TS APIs. Parsing strings at the type level (`"/users/:id"` -> `{ id: string }`) is possible but can slow the compiler and confuse teammates; use sparingly.

## Practical rules

- Start with simple concrete types; introduce generics when you see duplication that relates types.
- If a type needs three levels of conditional types to explain, a runtime schema or a simpler API is often better.
- Keep exported generics readable: name parameters meaningfully (`TItem`, `TKey`) when there are several.
- Type tests (`expectTypeOf` in vitest, `tsd`) protect complex types.
- Variance: function parameter positions are contravariant under `strictFunctionTypes`; `readonly` arrays are covariant. If you get confusing assignability errors, this is usually why.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Can you build **reusable, safe abstractions** without falling into type gymnastics? Expect live coding of generic helpers and questions about utility types.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. What are generics and why use them?

**Model answer.** Type parameters that let a function, class or type work over many types while preserving the relationship between them: `first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined` returns exactly the element type. They provide reuse without `any`. A good generic relates at least two positions; a type parameter used once is usually unnecessary.

### 2. How do constraints work?

**Model answer.** `T extends X` limits which types may be supplied, and lets the body use members of `X` safely, e.g. `T extends { length: number }`. With `K extends keyof T` I can write type-safe property access where the return type is `T[K]`.

### 3. Explain `Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit` and `Record` and where you use them.

**Model answer.** `Partial` makes all properties optional (PATCH payloads), `Pick` selects some keys (a public view), `Omit` removes keys (hiding passwords, creation DTOs without ids), and `Record<K, V>` builds a dictionary type with known keys. They're mapped types in the standard library; I derive related types from one source rather than redeclaring shapes.

### 4. What is a conditional type and what does `infer` do?

**Model answer.** `T extends U ? X : Y` selects a type depending on assignability, and distributes over unions when T is a naked type parameter. `infer` introduces a type variable inside the `extends` clause to capture part of the matched type, as in `T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T` or `ReturnType`.

### 5. How would you type a function `get(obj, key)` that returns the property value?

**Model answer.** `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`. `keyof T` ensures the key exists, and the indexed access type `T[K]` gives the precise type of that property, so `get(user, "age")` is `number` while an invalid key is a compile error.

### 6. How do you keep types in sync with runtime validation?

**Model answer.** Define a schema once with zod or similar and derive the TypeScript type from it with `z.infer`. For constants, use `as const` and derive unions with `typeof X[number]`. Duplicated hand-written types and validators drift apart.

### 7. When are advanced types a bad idea?

**Model answer.** When they are harder to read than the problem they solve, slow down the compiler, or produce error messages nobody can decode. If a utility type needs recursion and multiple conditional layers, I'd prefer a simpler API, runtime checks, or documented tests of the types, because a type the team can't maintain is a liability.

## Rapid-fire

- **`Omit` vs `Exclude`?** Omit removes keys from an object type; Exclude removes members from a union.
- **How to get an array's element type?** `T[number]`.
- **`ReturnType<typeof fn>`?** The function's return type.
- **`keyof typeof obj`?** Union of an object's keys.
- **Make props deeply readonly?** A recursive mapped type, or `as const` for literals.

keyPoints: Generics relate types across a signature, avoiding any and duplication; constrain them with extends and infer them from arguments.
keyof, indexed access T[K] and constraints enable type-safe property access and helpers like pick and get.
Utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, Awaited) derive new types from a single source of truth.
Mapped types transform every property; conditional types with infer extract or choose types; template literal types build string unions.
Prefer simple, readable types and runtime schemas over clever type-level programming.

options: function get(obj: any, key: string): any
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]
function get<T>(obj: T, key: string): T
function get(obj: object, key: keyof object): unknown
check.q: Which signature correctly types a property getter whose return type depends on the key?
check.why: K is constrained to keys of T and the return type T[K] reflects exactly the selected property's type.

options: A union of User and string
check.why: Omit removes the listed keys from an object type, commonly used to expose a public view of a model.

options: Captures the promise's resolved type as R during matching
check.q: What does infer do in T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T?
check.why: infer introduces a type variable bound by pattern matching so you can extract inner types.

lessons.title: TypeScript in practice: config, modules, errors and patterns
lessons.summary: A sound tsconfig, runtime validation at the edges, error handling with Result types, type-safe APIs and the mistakes that make TypeScript codebases brittle.

parts.label: Configuration and tooling
parts.body:
## A sensible tsconfig

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "noEmit": true
  }
}
```

- `strict` is non-negotiable for new code. For migrating a JS codebase: enable `allowJs`/`checkJs`, convert file by file, turn strict flags on one at a time.
- `isolatedModules` and `verbatimModuleSyntax` make each file compilable alone (required by Babel, esbuild, SWC, Vite): use `import type { X }` for type-only imports.
- `noEmit` when a bundler transpiles and `tsc` is only the type checker (`tsc --noEmit` in CI); the type check and the transpile are separate steps.
- `skipLibCheck` speeds up builds by not checking `.d.ts` files of dependencies.
- **Path aliases** (`paths`) need matching bundler/test config.
- **Project references** and incremental builds for monorepos.

## Linting and formatting

ESLint with `typescript-eslint` catches what the compiler doesn't: `no-floating-promises`, `no-explicit-any`, `no-unnecessary-condition`, `consistent-type-imports`, `switch-exhaustiveness-check`. Prettier handles formatting. Run both plus `tsc --noEmit` in CI and as a pre-commit hook.

## Declaration files and third-party code

Libraries ship `.d.ts` files or have types in `@types/*`. For an untyped module, write a minimal `declare module "x";` and tighten later; contribute types upstream when you can. Augment global or module types with declaration merging (`declare global { interface Window { analytics: ... } }`), keeping augmentations in one `types/` folder.

parts.label: Patterns for robust code
parts.body:
## Validate at the boundary, trust inside

All data crossing the boundary (HTTP bodies, environment variables, `localStorage`, query strings, message queues, third-party APIs) is `unknown`. Parse it once with a schema and use precise types inside.

```ts
import { z } from "zod";
const Env = z.object({ DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(), PORT: z.coerce.number().default(3000) });
export const env = Env.parse(process.env);        // fails fast at startup with a readable error
type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;           // one source of truth for type and validator
```

## Errors: exceptions vs Result types

TypeScript does not track thrown errors in function signatures, and a `catch` variable is `unknown`. Two approaches:

1. **Exceptions** for truly exceptional conditions (bugs, I/O failures), caught at a boundary. Always narrow: `if (e instanceof HttpError) ...`. Create error classes with a `cause`.
2. **Result values** for expected failures (validation, not found), making handling explicit and visible in types: `type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }` (libraries: neverthrow, effect).

Pick one convention per layer. Don't mix `null` returns, thrown errors and result objects arbitrarily.

## Model the domain with types

- **Discriminated unions** for states and results.
- **Branded types** for IDs and units (`UserId`, `Cents`) so they can't be mixed.
- **Readonly** by default for data (`readonly` props, `ReadonlyArray`) to discourage mutation.
- **Enums vs unions**: `const` arrays with `as const` and a derived union give runtime values and types from one place.
- **Exhaustive switches** via `never`.
- **Opaque constructors / smart constructors**: `createEmail(s): Result<Email, Error>` ensures an `Email` is always valid.

## Typing React and APIs (brief)

- Components: `function Card({ title, children }: { title: string; children: React.ReactNode })`; derive props from elements with `React.ComponentProps<"button">`.
- Generic components: `function List<T>({ items, render }: { items: T[]; render: (t: T) => ReactNode })`.
- Hooks: let `useState` infer, or give the generic when starting `null`: `useState<User | null>(null)`.
- End-to-end types: share schemas or generated clients (OpenAPI codegen, tRPC, GraphQL codegen) between server and client, so a backend change breaks the client build rather than production.

## Common mistakes

| mistake | better |
|---|---|
| `as` casts to silence errors | narrow with guards or validate with a schema |
| `any` everywhere | `unknown` plus narrowing; fix the root cause |
| `!` non-null assertions | handle the null case |
| enums with numeric values | string literal unions or `as const` objects |
| over-annotating locals | rely on inference; annotate public APIs |
| giant, deeply conditional types | simplify, split, or use runtime schemas |
| optional properties for state | discriminated unions |
| `Function` / `Object` / `{}` types | specific signatures; `Record<string, unknown>` |
| types that mirror the database 1:1 for the UI | separate DTO/view models |
| ignoring `tsc` errors in CI | make type check a required check |

## Performance of the compiler

Slow `tsc` usually means huge unions, deeply recursive types, many inferred generics or a single giant project. Measure with `tsc --extendedDiagnostics`/`--generateTrace`, use project references, and avoid types that expand to thousands of members.

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Seniority shows in how you **configure, validate and structure** TypeScript projects, and in your judgement about when types help and when they get in the way.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. How would you introduce TypeScript into a large JavaScript codebase?

**Model answer.** Incrementally. Add `tsconfig` with `allowJs` and `checkJs` off, then convert leaf modules and shared utilities first, start with `strict` off per directory or use `// @ts-check` with JSDoc on hot files, and tighten flags gradually. Add types at boundaries (API clients, domain models) first since they give the most value, set up CI type checking early, and track the count of `any`/`@ts-ignore` to drive down.

### 2. How do you type API responses safely?

**Model answer.** Treat the body as `unknown`, validate with a schema, and infer the type from it. Alternatively generate clients from OpenAPI or share types through tRPC/GraphQL codegen so the contract is checked at build time. A bare `as ApiResponse` cast doesn't verify anything.

### 3. How do you handle errors in TypeScript?

**Model answer.** `catch` variables are `unknown`, so I narrow with `instanceof`. For unexpected failures I use exceptions with custom error classes and a central handler; for expected failures such as validation or not found I prefer Result-style return values or discriminated unions, so callers must handle them and types document them. I choose one convention per layer.

### 4. What are branded types and when do you use them?

**Model answer.** A technique to make structurally identical types incompatible by intersecting with a phantom property: `type UserId = string & { __brand: "UserId" }`. It prevents mixing IDs or units (cents vs dollars) at compile time without runtime cost, created via validated constructors or a controlled cast at the boundary.

### 5. `enum` or union of string literals?

**Model answer.** I mostly use string literal unions (or `as const` objects), which have no runtime code, serialise naturally, and work well with JSON. Regular enums generate runtime objects, numeric enums allow arbitrary numbers to be assigned, and `isolatedModules` complicates `const enum`. If I need the values at runtime, I derive the union from a `const` array.

### 6. Why might `tsc` be slow and what do you do?

**Model answer.** Large unions, deeply recursive conditional types, heavy inference and a single huge project. I profile with `--extendedDiagnostics` and `--generateTrace`, split into project references with incremental builds, simplify the offending types, turn on `skipLibCheck`, and use a faster transpiler (esbuild/SWC) separately from the type check.

## Rapid-fire

- **Type-only import syntax?** `import type { X } from "./x"`.
- **Replace `!`?** A real null check or an assertion function.
- **Where do type errors surface in CI?** `tsc --noEmit`.
- **One source for type and validator?** A zod schema with `z.infer`.
- **What does `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` change?** `arr[i]` becomes `T | undefined`.

complexity.time: O(project size), minutes in huge repos

keyPoints: Use strict plus noUncheckedIndexedAccess; type-check with tsc --noEmit in CI and transpile separately; use import type.
Validate all external data with a schema at the boundary and derive static types from it.
Handle expected failures with discriminated unions or Result types, unexpected ones with exceptions narrowed from unknown.
Model the domain: discriminated unions, branded types, readonly data, smart constructors and exhaustive switches.
Avoid casts, any, non-null assertions and heroic type-level code; share types or schemas end to end.

options: Types are erased at runtime and cannot verify what the server actually sent
check.q: Why validate JSON from an API even though you declared a TypeScript interface?
check.why: The compiler trusts your declaration; only runtime validation can confirm the data matches, and it can derive the static type.

options: Adds undefined to the type of indexed access like arr[0]
Checks array length at compile time
check.why: Indexing may go out of bounds at runtime, so the option makes the result T | undefined, forcing a check.

check.q: Which is the best way to prevent passing an OrderId where a UserId is expected (both strings)?
check.why: Intersecting each string with a distinct phantom brand makes them incompatible at compile time with no runtime cost.
